implementation_notes: For the pattern's object intent - an interface with one or more operations - the ES2015 class that holds the wrapped object and delegates is the clearest realization: only the changed methods are overridden, the rest forward explicitly, and the class remains substitutable for the wrapped object in duck-typed code. It is the form to bind when callers pass objects around (repositories, clients, stores) and the chain has to look like the component; the TC39 decorator syntax is a different concept (it customises class members at definition time and cannot wrap an arbitrary object instance), and the built-in Proxy is the dynamic form that removes pass-through code at the cost of identity and introspection.

variants.name: Class implementing the same contract, delegating to the wrapped object
variants.idiom_name: class X implements/duck-types the component, stores the inner instance in the constructor and forwards the unchanged methods
variants.implementation_notes: For the pattern's object intent - an interface with one or more operations - the ES2015 class that holds the wrapped object and delegates is the clearest realization: only the changed methods are overridden, the rest forward explicitly, and the class remains substitutable for the wrapped object in duck-typed code. It is the form to bind when callers pass objects around (repositories, clients, stores) and the chain has to look like the component; the TC39 decorator syntax is a different concept (it customises class members at definition time and cannot wrap an arbitrary object instance), and the built-in Proxy is the dynamic form that removes pass-through code at the cost of identity and introspection.
pitfalls: Pass-through methods are maintained by hand: JavaScript has no interface to enforce them, so a method added to the inner type is silently missing from the decorator until a call fails.
Private state (#field/WeakMap) of the inner object is unreachable and `instanceof` checks against the wrapped class fail - code that branches on the concrete type changes behaviour once wrapped.

Using `new Proxy(inner, { get })` would remove the pass-through code, but it changes object identity and break `===`/WeakMap keys and type assumptions; choose it only when the extra interception is genuinely dynamic.

variants.name: Higher-order function wrapper with call forwarding
variants.idiom_name: function that takes a function and returns a wrapper calling original.apply(this, arguments) before/after its own work
variants.implementation_notes: When the component is effectively one function, the wrapper is a function too: withLogging(fn) returns a wrapper that performs its work and forwards with `fn.apply(this, arguments)`, preserving the receiver and the full argument list (javascript.info calls this call forwarding). Decorators built this way - cachingDecorator, withRetry, withTimeout - are reusable on any function of the same shape, compose by nesting and need no classes; they remain the only option for standalone functions because the TC39 decorator syntax applies to class members only. Reach for the class variant when the contract has several methods, since threading each one through functions costs more than a delegating class.
pitfalls: A wrapper is a different function object: properties hung on the original (fn.callsSeen) and its name in stack traces are lost unless copied with Object.defineProperty or a Proxy.
Arrow functions in the wrapper drop the caller's `this`; use a regular function plus apply/call forwarding, or bind deliberately.
Async wrappers must return or await the inner promise (and use try/finally for cleanup), otherwise rejections and timers escape the decoration.
